generator_view.scenario: You are hosting a chocolate tasting next month and want an affordable lineup, but first want to understand what guests would actually be tasting. The frozen shopping set contains five exact listings: a 22.98-dollar Green & Black's variety pack whose title and detail describe eight 3.17-ounce bars spanning 85-percent dark, 70-percent dark, milk, milk with almonds and white, while Product Dimensions reports only 3.17 ounces and the selected flavor field says 70-percent cacao; a 5.39-dollar single Lindt white bar with no mass shown; a 9.58-dollar Lindt Classic milk listing titled 4.4 ounces and two pieces while Product Dimensions reports 4.4 ounces; one 7.99-dollar Ritter Sport 61-percent 100-gram bar rated 55 percent over four reviews; and an 8.99-dollar Chocolove ruby listing titled two bars and selected as a 3.1-ounce two-pack while Product Dimensions reports 3.1 ounces, rated 78 percent over twelve reviews. Background pages describe beans, nibs, chocolate liquor, cocoa butter, conching, white chocolate and the disputed ruby category. Three community pages contain only one planned local blind caramel comparison, place-specific hot-cocoa preferences and a lay discussion of smell, texture, color and temperature in flavor. No source supplies current delivered labels, complete ingredients and allergens for all offers, a matched bar tasting or a universal percentage-to-quality ranking.
generator_view.target: Audit what every frozen seller, concept and community source can and cannot establish for an affordable chocolate tasting. Build an exact-offer matrix with literal pack, mass, price, percentage, category, rating and unknown fields, show conditional arithmetic, and preserve all quantity conflicts. Explain the general bean-to-liquor pathway, cocoa solids and butter, and conching without inventing exact process histories or a longer-is-better rule. Explain why white chocolate contains a cocoa-derived fat despite lacking nonfat cocoa solids, why real-versus-fake depends on definitions and preferences, and why ruby remains a disputed category rather than a title-proven fourth natural type. Then design a small category-aware tasting that separates educational contrasts from matched comparisons, verifies guest and label constraints, masks cues, standardizes comparable servings and records sensory difference separately from liking. End with a lowest-commitment passing lineup, verified control, reduced lineup or deferral procedure without a universal product, percentage or category winner.
